opus-5.5.text:
That's a good place to start, because the term itself has a history that people often overlook. "Embodied" as a concept goes back decades, to cognitive science and to people like Rodney Brooks at MIT in the late eighties and nineties, who argued that intelligence can't be separated from a body interacting with the physical world. So the idea isn't new. What's new is how the label came back into fashion.

In the U.S., I'd say the revival happened in roughly two waves. The first was in the academic community, especially in computer vision, around 2017 to 2019. People realized that learning from static internet images, labeling a photo as "cat" or "dog," was hitting its limits. So groups at Stanford, Berkeley, Meta's FAIR lab, and the Allen Institute started building simulated environments where an agent could move around, look at things from different angles, and pick objects up. They called this "embodied AI," and they held workshops at CVPR under that name. At that stage it was largely a research framing: let's move from passive perception to active agents.

The second wave came after large language models took off. Once people saw what GPT-style models could do with language, the obvious question was: can this kind of general intelligence get into the physical world? That's when the term moved out of academia and into industry and investment. Suddenly you had humanoid robot companies, foundation models for robotics, and huge funding rounds, and "embodied AI" became the umbrella term for all of it.

Interestingly, in the U.S. people now often just say "robot learning" or "physical AI." "Embodied AI" as a buzzword has actually become even more prominent in China than in America. Here it's almost become the name of a whole industry.

My own view is that the term captures something real. Language models learned from the enormous amount of text humans have produced. Physical intelligence has no equivalent internet of data, since nobody has recorded billions of hours of robots folding clothes or turning screwdrivers. So embodiment isn't just "put a model in a robot." It forces us to rethink where data comes from, how to use simulation and synthetic data, and how perception, reasoning, and action fit together. That's why I think it's one of the most important, and hardest, frontiers right now.

r001.rationale: The response says “embodied AI” became an umbrella term for industry activity and describes a research framing, but it does not clearly say the term crystallized a shared consensus.

fable-5.1.text:
The term actually has a longer history than most people realize. "Embodied intelligence" goes back decades in cognitive science and robotics — Rodney Brooks at MIT was arguing in the late 1980s that intelligence can't be separated from a body interacting with the physical world. That was a reaction against the symbolic AI of the time, which treated intelligence as pure reasoning over abstract representations.

But the recent explosion of the term in the US, I think, comes from a very specific convergence. Around 2022 and 2023, large language models and multimodal models suddenly showed that you could get surprisingly general capabilities from scale. People in the robotics community looked at that and asked: why hasn't robotics had its ChatGPT moment? And the answer most people landed on was data. Language models learned from the entire internet. Robots have no internet of physical interaction to learn from.

So "embodied AI" became the label for this new ambition — taking the foundation model paradigm and extending it to agents that perceive, act, and receive feedback in the physical world. Groups at Google DeepMind with RT-1 and RT-2, Stanford, Berkeley, and then startups like Figure and Physical Intelligence all started framing their work this way. Nvidia also pushed it very hard commercially, because for them it's the next large compute market after language.

What I find interesting is the shift in emphasis. Classical robotics was about control, planning, precision — engineering disciplines. Embodied AI, as the Americans use it now, is really a learning problem. The body is treated as a source of data and grounding, and the question becomes how you collect enough diverse physical experience, or simulate it, to train a general policy.

I'd also say the term carries a certain philosophical claim, which is that you cannot get true general intelligence from text alone. A model that has only read about cups has never felt that a cup can slip or spill. Whether that claim is right is still an open debate, but it's a big part of why the term resonates — it suggests a path to AGI that passes through the physical world rather than around it.

From the Chinese side, we adopted the translation 具身智能 very quickly, and in some ways the concept fits even better here, because China has the manufacturing base and hardware supply chain. So the US named the direction, but the race to realize it is genuinely global.

r001.rationale: The response says “embodied AI” became a label for a new ambition and describes a widely shared view that data is robotics’ main obstacle. It does not clearly say the term crystallized a shared consensus.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that “embodied AI” reflects a shift in how we think about intelligence. Instead of asking only whether an AI can recognize an image or generate an answer, we ask whether it can perceive an environment, act within it, and learn from the consequences.

The word “embodied” emphasizes that intelligence is connected to a body. What you can sense and how you can move affect what you learn. A robot picking up a cup, for example, has to connect visual perception with movement, contact, and feedback. Recognizing the cup is only one part of the problem.

So I wouldn’t interpret the emergence of the term in the United States as the sudden invention of an entirely new field. It brings together questions that robotics and AI have long explored, while putting the interaction between perception, action, and learning at the center.

r001.rationale: The response describes embodied AI as a shift that brings together longstanding questions, but does not say the term crystallizes a shared consensus in the United States.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the emergence of the term “embodied AI” reflects a shift in how people frame the problem of intelligence. Instead of asking only whether an AI can process information or generate answers, we ask whether it can perceive an environment, take action, and learn from the consequences.

The emphasis is on that interaction. If a robot wants to pick up a cup, recognizing the cup is only one part of the task. It also has to decide how to approach it, how to grasp it, and how to adjust if the cup moves or the grasp slips. Perception and action have to work together.

So I would understand “embodied AI” as a research perspective, rather than simply a new name for robots. It brings attention to intelligence that develops through interaction with an environment. That environment can be physical or simulated; the central question is how an agent connects what it perceives with what it does.

r001.rationale: The response frames “embodied AI” as a shift in perspective about intelligence and interaction, but does not say the term crystallized a shared consensus in the United States.
